MEDI2200 · Week 12 · Lecture module — Glucose metabolism (Dr Christine Chiu)

Glucose Metabolism — burning it, banking it, making it

One molecule of glucose, followed all the way: trapped in the cell, split by glycolysis, decarboxylated to acetyl-CoA, stripped of electrons by the TCA cycle, and cashed in as ATP by the electron transport chain. Then the other direction: how the liver stores glucose as glycogen and makes it from scratch when stores run out.

Covers chapters 1–10 of the iLearn module Figures 16 plates from the module Recall after every section

How to use this guide

Every subsection has a reference code like §5.2 — quote it to go deeper on exactly that piece. Each figure from your material appears as a numbered Plate with a Label Key decoding what's in it. The coloured tags carry the extras:

Reasoning
The why behind each step.
Memory hook
A trick to lock it in for the exam.
Clinical / real-world
What happens when a step fails.
🤔 Predict
Pause and guess before revealing — the guess is what makes it stick.
§01 Introduction · 2 Energy

Energy & redox

Metabolism means moving electrons downhill and catching the energy they release.

Food contains carbohydrates, proteins and lipids. These are digested to their monomers (sugars, amino acids, fatty acids) and absorbed through the gut. Then they are either metabolised for energy (ATP), used to build structural or functional molecules (proteins, cholesterol), or stored for later (glycogen, fat). This lecture deals only with carbohydrates; protein and lipid metabolism come next year. Two learning objectives: (1) describe the pathways of glucose oxidation (glycolysis, Krebs cycle, electron transport chain, ATP generation), and (2) explain the pathways of glucose storage and synthesis.

Oxidation and reduction

Breaking down glucose breaks chemical bonds and transfers electrons, and that releases energy. Most metabolic reactions are oxidation–reduction (redox) reactions. About 50% of the energy is conserved as ATP and as reduced electron carriers (NADH), and the rest is released as heat.

  • Oxidation = loss of electrons (often with H). Glucose is oxidised.
  • Reduction = gain of electrons. NAD⁺ is reduced to NADH (the module's flip-card).
🤔 Predict · the module's self-check

When electrons are transferred from a carbohydrate to NAD⁺, has the carbohydrate been oxidised or reduced?

Oxidised. It has lost electrons, and NAD⁺ has gained them (been reduced to NADH). Redox always comes in pairs: one partner's oxidation is the other's reduction.
Memory hook · OIL RIG

Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons). Fuel gets oxidised; carriers (NAD⁺, FAD) get reduced; O₂ is reduced to water at the end.

§0.1High-energy molecules — ATP, NAD⁺, FAD

ATP is the common currency of metabolic energy because it drives many energy-requiring reactions. Its tail of three phosphates is joined by phosphoanhydride bonds, and breaking those bonds releases energy that powers reactions. NAD⁺ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) and FAD (flavin adenine dinucleotide) are the main redox coenzymes. They accept electrons and carry them to the electron transport chain, where the electrons are used to power ATP production. All three are drawn in Plate 0.1.

Label Key — energy and electron carriers
Phosphoanhydride bonds (boxed)
The links between the phosphates. Breaking them (ATP → ADP + Pᵢ) releases energy, partly because the crowded negative charges repel and the products are more stable.
Ribose · adenine
The sugar and base of the nucleotide. The same adenosine "handle" also appears in NAD⁺ and FAD.
ATP
The short-term energy currency. It is spent within seconds of being made, not stored.
NAD⁺
Accepts 2 electrons + H⁺ on its nicotinamide ring to become NADH. It is made from niacin (vitamin B3).
FAD
Accepts 2 electrons + 2 H⁺ on its flavin ring to become FADH₂. It is made from riboflavin (vitamin B2).
Reasoning · why not make ATP directly from glucose?

Oxidising glucose all at once (burning it) releases its energy as a burst of heat that nothing can capture. Cells strip the electrons off in small steps and load them onto carriers (NADH, FADH₂). The carriers then pass the electrons down the ETC in more small steps, each one pumping a few protons (§5). Releasing the energy in small, matched portions is how the cell keeps about half of it instead of losing it all as heat.

§0.2Energy in food

Food energy isn't measured in ATP. It is measured in joules or calories: the heat released when a sample is completely burned (oxidised). The values for each fuel class are in Plate 0.2. (The module then shows nutrition labels and asks you to read the energy off them.)

Label Key — fuel values
Fats — 38 kJ/g (9 kcal/g)
More than twice carbohydrate. Fatty acids are more reduced (more C–H bonds, less oxygen), so they have more electrons left to give.
Carbohydrates — 17 kJ/g (4 kcal/g)
Already partly oxidised (lots of –OH groups).
Proteins — 17 kJ/g (4 kcal/g)
Same as carbohydrate.
Alcohol — 29 kJ/g (7 kcal/g)
An energy-dense fuel that is often forgotten.
Note: 1 Cal = 1 kcal; 1 kcal = 4.2 kJ
The nutritional "Calorie" (capital C) is the kilocalorie: the energy needed to warm 1 kg of water by 1 °C.
Worked example · reading a nutrition label (the module's "Tim Tam" question)

Australian labels list energy in kJ. Suppose a label lists 400 kJ per biscuit (an illustrative figure; read the real one off your pack). How many Calories is that?

  1. Conversion: 1 kcal = 4.2 kJ, so kcal = kJ ÷ 4.2.
  2. 400 ÷ 4.2 ≈ 95 kcal.
  3. Since 1 Cal = 1 kcal, that is ≈ 95 Calories.
  4. Cross-check from macronutrients: if the label lists 12 g carbohydrate, 5 g fat and 1 g protein, then 12×17 + 5×38 + 1×17 = 204 + 190 + 17 = 411 kJ, which agrees with the label.

Method: divide kJ by 4.2 to get Calories. Pick the module's option closest to the label value of the real product.

R Recall — energy & redox
  • Share of energy conserved as ATP/NADH — about 50% (rest is heat)
  • Electrons moved from carbohydrate to NAD⁺ — the carbohydrate is oxidised
  • ATP's energy-rich bonds — phosphoanhydride bonds
  • Main redox coenzymes — NAD⁺ and FAD
  • Fat energy content — 38 kJ/g (9 kcal/g)
  • Carbohydrate and protein energy — 17 kJ/g (4 kcal/g)
  • 1 kcal = 4.2 kJ = 1 Calorie
§13 · Carbohydrates

Carbohydrates & glucose transport

Water-soluble fuel that needs a door to get in.

Carbohydrates contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. Their many –OH groups make them polar and highly water-soluble. The simplest monosaccharides have three carbons, but hexoses (e.g. glucose) and pentoses (e.g. ribose) are the most common. Two monosaccharides joined by a glycosidic bond make a disaccharide. Long chains are polysaccharides: starches (amylose and amylopectin) in grains are the main dietary carbohydrate, and in animals glycogen is the storage form of glucose.

Glucose transport

Dietary carbohydrate is digested to glucose, which enters the bloodstream and travels to the tissues. It enters cells by facilitated diffusion through a glucose transporter protein (GLUT). All cells have GLUTs, and there are many types. GLUT4, in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue, is insulin-dependent. All other GLUTs let glucose move down its concentration gradient without needing insulin. Plate 1.1 shows the five-step carrier cycle, which is the passive transporter from Week 10 §1.1.

Label Key — the five steps
1 · The carrier has a glucose binding site
Facing outside, where glucose is high.
2 · Glucose binds
Specific binding, like a substrate in an enzyme.
3 · …which changes the protein's shape
The alternating-access flip.
4 · …releasing the glucose
Into the cytosol, where glucose is low.
5 · The carrier returns to its original shape
Ready for the next glucose. No ATP is used, so this is passive.
High → low glucose concentration
The gradient sets the direction. Inside, hexokinase keeps glucose low by phosphorylating it (§2), so the gradient is maintained.
Clinical / real-world · GLUT4 and diabetes

Insulin signals through its RTK and the PI3K–Akt pathway (Week 11 §5.4) to move GLUT4 from intracellular vesicles to the plasma membrane (regulated traffic, Week 10 §4.5). That is how muscle and fat clear glucose after a meal. In type 2 diabetes this insertion is blunted (insulin resistance), so blood glucose stays high. Exercise moves GLUT4 to the membrane through an insulin-independent pathway, which is one reason activity improves glycaemic control.

R Recall — carbohydrates
  • Disaccharide bond — glycosidic bond
  • Main dietary polysaccharides — starches (amylose, amylopectin)
  • Animal storage polysaccharide — glycogen
  • Glucose enters cells by — facilitated diffusion via GLUTs
  • Insulin-dependent GLUT — GLUT4, in skeletal muscle and adipose
§24 · Glycolysis

Glycolysis

Spend 2 ATP, make 4, keep 2 and 2 NADH.

Glycolysis is the first pathway glucose enters. It is a central anaerobic pathway (no O₂ needed) found in all cells, from bacteria to humans. It has 10 steps, takes place in the cytosol, and is divided into two stages, which you can follow down Plate 2.1.

  • Energy-consuming (investment) phase, steps 1–5. Uses 2 ATP. On entry, hexokinase phosphorylates glucose to glucose-6-phosphate. The phosphate traps glucose in the cell and keeps cytosolic free glucose low, so glucose keeps flowing in from the blood down its gradient. G6P is then rearranged, phosphorylated again and cleaved into two 3-carbon molecules of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate.
  • Energy-yielding phase, steps 6–10. Each glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate is oxidised (making NADH), phosphorylated and rearranged into pyruvate (3 carbons), making ATP along the way.

Net result per glucose: 2 pyruvate + 2 ATP + 2 NADH (4 ATP made − 2 ATP spent).

Label Key — follow the numbers
① glucose → glucose-6-P (ATP → ADP)
Hexokinase. This is the trapping step, because phosphorylated sugars can't leave through GLUTs.
② → fructose-6-P
An isomerisation that sets up a symmetrical split.
③ → fructose-1,6-bisP (ATP → ADP)
Phosphofructokinase (PFK-1). The committed, rate-limiting step and the main control point.
④ → DHAP + glyceraldehyde-3-P
Aldolase splits the 6-carbon sugar into two 3-carbon sugars.
⑤ DHAP → glyceraldehyde-3-P
Triose phosphate isomerase, so both halves continue: from here every step happens ×2.
⑥ 2 NAD⁺ → 2 NADH
The oxidation step, giving 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate. NAD⁺ must be regenerated for this step to continue (§7).
⑦ 2 ADP → 2 ATP
The first ATP payback (substrate-level phosphorylation).
⑧ → 2-phosphoglycerate · ⑨ −H₂O → phosphoenolpyruvate
Rearrange and dehydrate to create a high-energy phosphate.
⑩ 2 ADP → 2 ATP → 2 pyruvate
Pyruvate kinase. The second ATP payback, and in profit.
Energy investment / energy generation phase
2 ATP in (steps 1, 3); 4 ATP + 2 NADH out (steps 6, 7, 10).
Glycolysis enzymes (from the module's table)
ReactionEnzymeReactionEnzyme
1Hexokinase6Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase
2Phosphoglucoisomerase7Phosphoglycerate kinase
3Phosphofructokinase8Phosphoglycerate mutase
4Aldolase9Enolase
5Triose phosphate isomerase10Pyruvate kinase
Memory hook · the enzyme order

"Hungry People Pay A Tip, Generous People Pay Extra Profit": Hexokinase, Phosphoglucoisomerase, Phosphofructokinase, Aldolase, Triose phosphate isomerase, Glyceraldehyde-3-P dehydrogenase, Phosphoglycerate kinase, Phosphoglycerate mutase, Enolase, Pyruvate kinase. The three irreversible kinases (1, 3, 10) are the ones gluconeogenesis has to bypass (§6.2).

Worked example · "what proportion of glucose's energy does glycolysis extract?" (module self-check)
  1. Net ATP from glycolysis: 4 made − 2 spent = 2 ATP.
  2. Complete aerobic oxidation of one glucose yields roughly 30–38 ATP (textbooks differ; ~32 is the modern estimate).
  3. Fraction: 2 ÷ 38 ≈ 5% (or 2 ÷ 32 ≈ 6%).
  4. So most of glucose's energy is still locked in the 2 pyruvate and 2 NADH, waiting for the mitochondrion (§3–§5).

Answer: about 5%. Glycolysis is fast but extracts very little energy.

Clinical / real-world · cells that live on glycolysis

Red blood cells have no mitochondria and rely entirely on glycolysis. In pyruvate kinase deficiency (step 10), RBCs run short of ATP, can't maintain their membranes, and are destroyed (haemolytic anaemia). Many cancers also favour glycolysis even with oxygen present (the Warburg effect). FDG-PET scans exploit step 1: the glucose analogue FDG is phosphorylated by hexokinase and then trapped, so tumours that take up glucose fastest light up.

R Recall — glycolysis
  • Location — cytosol; anaerobic
  • Number of steps — 10
  • Energy-consuming phase — steps 1–5, uses 2 ATP
  • Enzyme that traps glucose — hexokinase (→ glucose-6-phosphate)
  • 6-carbon sugar is cleaved into — two glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate
  • Energy-yielding phase — steps 6–10
  • Net yield per glucose — 2 pyruvate, 2 ATP, 2 NADH
  • Share of glucose energy extracted — about 5%
§35 · Pyruvate

Pyruvate — the crossroads

Oxygen decides: into the mitochondrion, or off to lactate.

Pyruvate sits at a branch point. With oxygen, it enters the mitochondria and goes on to oxidative phosphorylation. Without oxygen, it is fermented to lactate (§7). Plate 3.1 shows both branches in one cell.

Label Key — two routes
Glucose → glycolysis (NAD⁺ → NADH) → pyruvate
Common to both routes, in the cytosol.
Oxygen present → mitochondrion
Pyruvate → acetyl CoA (NAD⁺ → NADH, CO₂ released) → TCA cycle → NADH, FADH₂ → electron transport chain.
ATP ×3 (yellow)
Most of the ATP is made here, aerobically.
Carbon dioxide and water
The end products of full oxidation: CO₂ from the carbons, H₂O from O₂ accepting electrons.
Oxygen absent → fermentation → lactate
Pyruvate accepts electrons from NADH, which regenerates the NAD⁺ that glycolysis needs.
NADH ⇄ NAD⁺ loops (green/red arrows)
The key bookkeeping: glycolysis consumes NAD⁺ and must get it back, from the mitochondrion (aerobic) or from lactate formation (anaerobic).
Lactate → (green arrow out)
Exported to the blood and recycled by the liver (Cori cycle, §7).

Under aerobic conditions — pyruvate dehydrogenase

Pyruvate is carried from the cytosol into the mitochondrial matrix and converted into acetyl-CoA by pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH). Acetyl-CoA is a common product of carbohydrate, fat and protein metabolism. The conversion is an oxidative decarboxylation: it releases CO₂ and transfers electrons to NAD⁺, forming NADH. It is irreversible, so the carbon is now committed to oxidative phosphorylation or fatty-acid synthesis and can't go back to glucose.

PDH is regulated by substrate availability and by product inhibition, shown by the + and − arrows in Plate 3.2: it is inhibited by high acetyl-CoA and NADH and activated by NAD⁺ and CoA.

Label Key — reaction and control
Cell cytosol / cell mitochondria (dashed line)
The reaction happens inside the mitochondrion after pyruvate is transported in.
Pyruvate (CH₃–CO–COO⁻)
3 carbons in.
+ NAD⁺ + CoA (green +)
Substrates that also activate. When they are plentiful, the cell can take more electrons and carbon.
Acetyl CoA (CH₃–CO–S–CoA) + CO₂
2 carbons out on CoA, and 1 carbon lost as CO₂, permanently.
+ NADH + H⁺
The electrons captured, which go to the ETC (§5).
Red − arrows from acetyl CoA and NADH
Product inhibition: if products pile up, the TCA/ETC is backed up, so PDH slows down.
Reasoning · why irreversibility matters for the whole body

Because PDH can't run backwards, acetyl-CoA can't be turned back into glucose. That is why even-chain fatty acids, which are broken down to acetyl-CoA, can't support blood glucose during fasting, while lactate, amino acids and glycerol can (§6.2). PDH is the one-way gate between "carbohydrate" and "fuel for burning or fat-making", so it is tightly controlled by its products.

Clinical / real-world · thiamine and PDH

PDH needs thiamine (vitamin B1) as a cofactor. In thiamine deficiency (alcohol misuse, malnutrition), pyruvate can't enter the mitochondrion, so it builds up as lactate, and the brain, which depends on glucose oxidation, is starved: Wernicke's encephalopathy. This is why thiamine is given before glucose to at-risk patients. Inherited PDH deficiency similarly causes lactic acidosis and neurological damage.

R Recall — pyruvate
  • With O₂, pyruvate goes to — the mitochondrial matrix
  • Without O₂, pyruvate becomes — lactate
  • Enzyme converting pyruvate to acetyl-CoA — pyruvate dehydrogenase
  • Reaction type — oxidative decarboxylation (CO₂ out, NADH made)
  • Is the PDH step reversible? — no, it is irreversible
  • PDH inhibitors — acetyl-CoA and NADH
  • PDH activators — NAD⁺ and CoA
§46 · Tricarboxylic acid cycle

The TCA (Krebs) cycle

Two carbons in, two CO₂ out, and the electrons saved on carriers.

Acetyl-CoA is the common end product of glucose, fat and protein breakdown. It is processed through the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, also called the Krebs cycle, in the mitochondria. The cycle has 8 steps. It begins when acetyl-CoA condenses with oxaloacetate (OAA) to form citrate, and it ends by regenerating oxaloacetate to start the cycle again. Go round Plate 4.1 clockwise.

Label Key — the eight steps
1 · Acetyl-CoA + oxaloacetate → citrate (citrate synthase)
2C + 4C → 6C, and CoA-SH is released. This is the entry step.
2 · Citrate → cis-aconitate → isocitrate (aconitase)
Moves the –OH group into position for oxidation.
3 · Isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate (isocitrate dehydrogenase) [green]
NADH + first CO₂ (6C → 5C).
4 · α-ketoglutarate → succinyl-CoA (α-KG dehydrogenase) [green]
NADH + second CO₂ (5C → 4C). A PDH-like enzyme that also needs thiamine.
5 · Succinyl-CoA → succinate (succinyl-CoA synthetase) [green]
GTP (equivalent to ATP), by substrate-level phosphorylation.
6 · Succinate → fumarate (succinate dehydrogenase) [green]
FADH₂. This enzyme is embedded in the inner membrane and is also ETC complex II (Plate 5.1).
7 · Fumarate → L-malate (fumarase)
Adds water.
8 · Malate → oxaloacetate (malate dehydrogenase) [green]
NADH, and oxaloacetate is regenerated for the next turn.
Cell mitochondria (centre)
All in the matrix.

Per acetyl-CoA, the cycle produces 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂ and 1 GTP (the green boxes), plus 2 CO₂. Per glucose, double it, since one glucose gives 2 acetyl-CoA.

Memory hook · "Citrate Is Krebs' Starting Substrate For Making Oxaloacetate"

Citrate → Isocitrate → α-Ketoglutarate → Succinyl-CoA → Succinate → Fumarate → Malate → Oxaloacetate. The yields (NADH, NADH, GTP, FADH₂, NADH) fall on steps 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8.

A hub, not just a furnace

The TCA intermediates also feed biosynthesis of amino acids, fatty acids and other molecules, and they can be topped up from amino acids, fatty acids and glucose. Plate 4.2 maps the outlets.

Label Key — what leaves the cycle
Oxaloacetate → aspartate → asparagine, lysine, methionine, threonine (→ isoleucine), purines, pyrimidines
Amino acid and nucleotide synthesis.
Citrate → (cytosolic) acetyl-CoA → fatty acids, steroids, ketones
Citrate carries acetyl units out of the mitochondrion for fat and cholesterol synthesis in the fed state.
α-ketoglutarate → glutamate → glutamine, proline, arginine, pyrimidines
The amino-group hub (transamination).
Succinyl-CoA → porphyrins → haem
The first committed step of haem synthesis for haemoglobin and cytochromes.
Pyruvate → oxaloacetate
Refills the cycle when intermediates are drawn off (pyruvate carboxylase, §6.2).

Regulation

The cycle is regulated by substrate availability and inhibition. Oxaloacetate and NAD⁺ increase activity; citrate and NADH inhibit it. Whether the body is fed or fasting also sets the cycle's activity.

Reasoning · NADH is the brake

The cycle's job is to load electrons onto NAD⁺. If NADH is already high (the ETC is full, often because ADP is low, §5.2), there is nowhere to put more electrons, so the dehydrogenases slow down. The same signal, NAD⁺ versus NADH, runs through PDH, the TCA cycle and the ETC, which keeps all three in step.

R Recall — TCA cycle
  • Location — mitochondrial matrix
  • Number of steps — 8
  • First step — acetyl-CoA + oxaloacetate → citrate
  • Yield per acetyl-CoA — 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP
  • TCA activators — oxaloacetate and NAD⁺
  • TCA inhibitors — citrate and NADH
  • Succinyl-CoA is a precursor of — haem (porphyrins)
§57 · Electron transport chain

The ETC & ATP synthase

Electrons fall, protons are pumped, the turbine turns.

Oxidative phosphorylation turns the energy captured from glucose (as NADH and FADH₂) into ATP. It happens in the mitochondria, specifically on the inner mitochondrial membrane, which carries all the components needed: the electron transport chain (ETC) and the enzyme complex ATP synthase.

§5.1Building the proton gradient

The ETC has four enzyme complexes (I–IV) that act as proton pumps. They move H⁺ from the matrix into the space between the inner and outer membranes. Two coenzymes, ubiquinone (Q) and cytochrome c, carry electrons between the complexes. Plate 5.1 shows the start of the chain.

Label Key — the chain
Cell cytosol / outer mitochondrial membrane
The outer membrane is permeable to small ions, so the gradient that matters is across the inner membrane.
Crista space (intermembrane space)
Where protons are pumped. It becomes the high-[H⁺], positive side.
Inner mitochondrial membrane
Impermeable to H⁺, which is essential, since otherwise the gradient would leak away.
Matrix · 2 e⁻ from NADH → complex I (green, left)
NADH hands over its electrons and complex I pumps H⁺.
Succinate dehydrogenase · FADH₂ → FAD + 2 e⁻ · citric acid cycle
Complex II, the TCA enzyme from step 6. It feeds electrons into Q but pumps no protons, which is why FADH₂ yields less ATP than NADH.
Ubiquinone (Q)
A mobile, lipid-soluble carrier that shuttles electrons to complex III.
Complex III (green, centre) → cytochrome c (C)
Complex III pumps H⁺; cytochrome c, a small water-soluble protein, carries electrons on to complex IV.
Complex IV (blue, right; cut off)
Passes electrons to O₂, the final acceptor, making H₂O, and pumps H⁺.
H⁺ arrows
Protons pumped from matrix to intermembrane space at complexes I, III and IV.

Take-home message: the step-by-step transfer of electrons builds a proton gradient (an electrochemical gradient) between the mitochondrial matrix and the intermembrane space.

Clinical / real-world · poisons and uncouplers

Cyanide and carbon monoxide block complex IV. Electrons can't reach O₂, the gradient collapses, ATP production stops, and cells switch to glycolysis and pour out lactate. Uncouplers (the old diet drug DNP; thermogenin/UCP1 in brown fat) let H⁺ leak back without passing through ATP synthase. The ETC runs flat out but the energy comes out as heat. That is how newborns keep warm, and why DNP overdose causes fatal hyperthermia.

§5.2ATP synthase — the turbine

ATP synthase is an F-type transmembrane pump (Week 10 §1.4) that works like a turbine. H⁺ ions flowing back down their electrochemical gradient, from the intermembrane space into the matrix, turn the turbine shaft, and the rotation drives the phosphorylation of ADP to ATP. This is oxidative phosphorylation. Find the parts in Plate 5.2.

Label Key — rotor, stator, head
Intermembrane space · H⁺
The high-[H⁺] reservoir built by the ETC.
F₀ proton pore and motor · c-ring · subunit a
H⁺ enters via a, binds the c-ring, and the ring rotates one step per proton, then the H⁺ exits into the matrix.
γ, ε (central stalk)
The rotating shaft fixed to the c-ring. Its off-centre shape squeezes the head as it turns.
α, β (F₁ ATP synthase / ATPase)
The catalytic head in the matrix. The β subunits cycle through shapes that bind ADP + Pᵢ, join them, then release ATP.
b, δ (stator)
A peripheral arm that holds the head still, so the shaft turns inside it instead of spinning the whole thing.
ADP + Pᵢ (red box) → ATP
The substrates in and product out. ATP is the usable energy for our cells.

ADP is the key regulator

ADP is the key feedback regulator of oxidative phosphorylation. When ADP enters the mitochondria, ATP synthase speeds up, which lowers the H⁺ gradient as protons are used. The smaller gradient then increases respiration, because the ETC works harder to rebuild it and O₂ use rises. When ADP runs out, ATP synthase stops, the gradient stays high, and oxygen uptake falls.

Reasoning · supply on demand

This is "respiratory control": the cell burns fuel only as fast as it uses ATP. Exercise uses ATP, ADP rises, ATP synthase runs, the gradient drops, the ETC speeds up, NADH is used up, and the TCA cycle and PDH speed up too (§3–§4). One signal, ADP, sets the pace of the whole chain back to glucose without any hormone.

§5.3Supplying ADP and phosphate

ATP synthesis needs ADP and Pᵢ inside the matrix, and some of the H⁺ gradient's energy is spent bringing them in from the cytosol. Two antiporters (Week 10 §1.2) do it, shown in Plate 5.3:

  • ATP/ADP antiporter: exports one newly made ATP and imports one cytosolic ADP.
  • HPO₄²⁻/OH⁻ antiporter (phosphate transporter): imports one phosphate and exports one OH⁻.
Label Key — paying for the import
H⁺ concentration gradient · membrane electric potential (+ outside, − matrix)
The two parts of the proton-motive force.
Translocation of H⁺ during electron transport
The ETC builds the gradient.
Phosphate transporter (HPO₄²⁻ in, OH⁻ out)
Exporting OH⁻ amounts to importing H⁺, so phosphate import is paid for by the pH part of the gradient.
ATP/ADP antiporter (ADP³⁻ in, ATP⁴⁻ out)
ATP carries one more negative charge than ADP. Swapping them moves one net negative charge out, driven by the voltage part of the gradient (outside is positive).
3 H⁺ → ATP synthase
Roughly 3 H⁺ per ATP made, plus about 1 more for transport, so ~4 H⁺ per ATP delivered to the cytosol.
Worked example · tallying ATP from one glucose (approximate)

Using modern estimates of ~2.5 ATP per NADH and ~1.5 per FADH₂ (each includes the proton cost of transport in Plate 5.3):

  1. Glycolysis: 2 ATP + 2 NADH.
  2. PDH (×2 pyruvate): 2 NADH.
  3. TCA (×2 acetyl-CoA): 6 NADH + 2 FADH₂ + 2 GTP.
  4. Total carriers: 10 NADH × 2.5 = 25; 2 FADH₂ × 1.5 = 3.
  5. Direct: 2 ATP + 2 GTP = 4. Sum: 25 + 3 + 4 = 32 ATP. Older textbooks using 3 and 2 per carrier get 36–38.

Answer: ~30–32 ATP per glucose, about 15× more than glycolysis alone (2 ATP), which is why §2's answer was ~5%.

R Recall — ETC & ATP synthase
  • Site of oxidative phosphorylation — inner mitochondrial membrane
  • ETC proton pumps — four complexes (I–IV)
  • Mobile electron carriers — ubiquinone and cytochrome c
  • Protons are pumped from — matrix to intermembrane space
  • ATP synthase type — F-type, works like a turbine
  • Energy for ATP synthase comes from — H⁺ flowing down its gradient into the matrix
  • Key feedback regulator — ADP
  • When ADP is depleted — ATP synthase stops; O₂ uptake falls
  • ADP import transporter — ATP/ADP antiporter
  • Phosphate import transporter — HPO₄²⁻/OH⁻ antiporter
§68 · Glucose storage and synthesis

Glycogen & gluconeogenesis

Bank it after meals, withdraw it between meals, make it from scratch in a fast.

§6.1Glycogenesis and glycogenolysis

Glycogen is the first line of defence against falling blood glucose. After eating, glucose is channelled into glycogen as a reserve to use between meals. Making glycogen is glycogenesis; breaking it down is glycogenolysis. Both happen mainly in liver and muscle. Follow the cycle in Plate 6.1.

  • Glycogenesis. Starts at glucose-6-phosphate, which is isomerised to glucose-1-P and activated to the sugar nucleotide UDP-glucose (using UTP). Glycogen synthase then adds it to the growing glycogen chain.
  • Glycogenolysis in the liver. When blood glucose falls between meals, the liver breaks glycogen down to maintain blood glucose for about 12–16 hours. Debranching enzyme removes glucose at the branch points, glycogen phosphorylase releases glucose-1-P, and after conversion to G6P, glucose-6-phosphatase removes the phosphate to release free glucose into the blood.
  • Glycogenolysis in muscle. Glycogen goes to glucose-6-phosphate for glycolysis during prolonged exercise. Muscle glycogen can't support blood glucose because muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase.
Label Key — the glycogen cycle
Glucose 6-P ⇄ glucose 1-P
The junction shared by glycolysis, glycogen and (liver) glucose release.
UTP → PPᵢ · UDP-glucose
Activation step. Breaking down PPᵢ makes it irreversible, so synthesis is pulled forward.
Glycogen synthase (and branching enzyme) → UDP
Lengthens chains and creates branches. More branches mean more ends to add to or remove from at once.
Glycogen phosphorylase (and debranching enzyme) · Pᵢ
Uses phosphate (not water) to cut off glucose-1-P, so the sugar comes off already phosphorylated, saving an ATP.
Glucose 6-phosphatase (liver) → glucose
Only the liver (and kidney) can release free glucose to the blood.
Glycolysis (ATP) (muscle) → pyruvate
Muscle keeps its glycogen for its own use.
Reasoning · why muscle won't share its glycogen

Once glucose is phosphorylated it can't leave the cell (§2). The liver has glucose-6-phosphatase to remove the phosphate; muscle doesn't. That makes muscle glycogen a private store for exercise and liver glycogen a store for the whole body, the brain especially, between meals.

Clinical / real-world · glycogen storage diseases

Von Gierke disease (glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency): the liver can't release glucose, so infants have severe fasting hypoglycaemia, an enlarged glycogen-packed liver, and lactic acidosis. McArdle disease (muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency): blood glucose is normal, but muscles cramp and fatigue in early exercise because they can't use their glycogen. The two diseases follow directly from the liver-versus-muscle split in Plate 6.1.

Where does blood glucose come from across a day?

Plate 6.2 tracks the three sources. Dietary glucose peaks after each meal; glycogenolysis covers the gaps between meals; gluconeogenesis takes over overnight and in longer fasts.

Label Key — three sources
Dietary (blue)
Spikes to ~100% just after breakfast, lunch and dinner.
Glycogenolysis (green)
Fills in as each meal is absorbed. This is the "between meals" source.
Gluconeogenesis (red)
Highest overnight and before breakfast, after the longest fast, when liver glycogen is running low.
Time axis: breakfast, 12.00 lunch, dinner, 24.00
A normal eating day. Stretch the fast and the red line takes over completely.

§6.2Gluconeogenesis — making new glucose

If a fast lasts longer than about 10 hours, the body gradually shifts from glycogenolysis to de novo synthesis of glucose, gluconeogenesis. It is essential for keeping blood glucose up in prolonged fasting or starvation, once glycogen stores are used up.

  • It is the opposite of glycolysis and shares many of the same enzymes.
  • It happens mainly in the liver, which has the special enzymes needed to get around glycolysis's irreversible steps (green in Plate 6.3).
  • Pyruvate is a common starting point. The main substrates are lactate, amino-acid carbon skeletons (e.g. alanine) and glycerol from triglyceride breakdown.
  • The energy to run it comes from oxidising fatty acids released from triglycerides.
Label Key — read from the bottom up
Lactate → pyruvate (NADH)
Lactate dehydrogenase in reverse; lactate arrives from muscle and red cells (Cori cycle, §7).
Alanine and a few other amino acids → pyruvate (glutamate ⇄ α-ketoglutarate)
Transamination removes the amino group, leaving the carbon skeleton.
Pyruvate carboxylase (mitochondrion; ATP, CO₂) [green]
Bypass 1a: pyruvate → oxaloacetate. It adds a carbon to get around pyruvate kinase.
Oxaloacetate ⇄ malate (export) · via transport of Glu, Asp, α-KG
Oxaloacetate can't cross the inner membrane, so it is shuttled out as malate (or aspartate), carrying NADH equivalents with it.
Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (CO₂, GTP → GDP) [green]
Bypass 1b: oxaloacetate → PEP. Removing the CO₂ pays for making the high-energy phosphate.
Glyceraldehyde 3-P ⇄ DHAP ← glycerol 3-phosphate ← glycerol (ATP)
Glycerol from fat enters halfway up.
Fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase [green]
Bypass 2: removes Pᵢ to get around PFK-1.
Glucose 6-phosphatase (endoplasmic reticulum) [green]
Bypass 3: removes Pᵢ to get around hexokinase and release free glucose. This is the same liver-only enzyme as Plate 6.1.
Citric acid cycle (dashed) · mitochondrion
Amino acids that enter as α-ketoglutarate, succinyl-CoA or fumarate feed in via oxaloacetate.
Memory hook · "Pathway Produces Fresh Glucose"

The four bypass enzymes, bottom to top: Pyruvate carboxylase, PEP carboxykinase, Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, Glucose-6-phosphatase. They replace glycolysis's three irreversible kinases: pyruvate kinase, PFK-1 and hexokinase.

Reasoning · why separate one-way enzymes in each direction?

If glycolysis and gluconeogenesis used the same enzymes at the irreversible steps, the cell couldn't run one without the other. Having different enzymes at those three points lets each direction be switched on or off separately, by insulin and glucagon. If both ran at full speed together, the cell would just burn ATP in a "futile cycle".

Clinical / real-world · metformin and alcohol

Metformin, the first-line type 2 diabetes drug, lowers blood glucose mainly by suppressing hepatic gluconeogenesis. Alcohol metabolism floods the liver with NADH, which pushes pyruvate to lactate and oxaloacetate to malate. That drains gluconeogenesis substrates, so a fasting binge drinker (whose glycogen is already gone) can become dangerously hypoglycaemic.

R Recall — storage & synthesis
  • Glycogen formation — glycogenesis
  • Glycogen breakdown — glycogenolysis
  • Activated sugar for glycogen synthesis — UDP-glucose
  • Chain-lengthening enzyme — glycogen synthase
  • Enzyme releasing glucose-1-P from glycogen — glycogen phosphorylase
  • Liver glycogen sustains blood glucose for — about 12–16 hours
  • Muscle can't release glucose because it lacks — glucose-6-phosphatase
  • Gluconeogenesis begins after — about 10 hours of fasting
  • Main site of gluconeogenesis — the liver
  • Gluconeogenic substrates — lactate, amino acids, glycerol
  • Gluconeogenesis is powered by — fatty-acid oxidation
§79 · Pyruvate revisited

No oxygen — lactate & the Cori cycle

Lactate isn't waste. It is a way to keep glycolysis running, and it gets paid back later.

When oxygen is absent or limited (e.g. in hard exercise), the ETC can't accept electrons, so pyruvate and NADH can't be oxidised in the mitochondrion. Tissues rely instead on anaerobic glycolysis. Pyruvate is converted to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase, and this reaction oxidises NADH back to NAD⁺, which glycolysis needs to keep going.

Label Key — the NAD⁺ loop
Glucose → (glycolysis) → 2 pyruvate · net 2 ATP
The only ATP made without oxygen.
2 NAD⁺ → 2 NADH (glycolysis)
Uses up NAD⁺ at step 6 (red box on the glycolysis diagram).
2 pyruvate → (fermentation) → 2 lactate · 2 NADH → 2 NAD⁺
Lactate dehydrogenase passes the electrons onto pyruvate, freeing NAD⁺.
Curved arrow back to glycolysis
The regenerated NAD⁺ returns to step 6, so glycolysis can keep running.
Reasoning · why make lactate at all?

A cell has only a small pool of NAD⁺. Without a way to reoxidise NADH, glycolysis would stop at step 6 within seconds and ATP production would fall to zero. Turning pyruvate into lactate gains no ATP directly. Its only job is to recycle NAD⁺ so the 2 ATP per glucose keep coming. Lactate is the price of fast, oxygen-free ATP.

The Cori cycle

Lactate made in muscle diffuses into the blood and travels to the liver, which converts it back to pyruvate and then to glucose by gluconeogenesis. The new glucose is released from the liver and taken up by other tissues, which oxidise it to regenerate energy. That loop is the Cori cycle, in Plate 7.2.

Label Key — liver ⇄ muscle
Muscle (right) · glycolysis · Glc-6-P → pyruvate → lactate
Working muscle short of O₂ exports lactate.
Lactate → lactate (blood)
Carried to the liver.
Liver (left) · lactate → pyruvate → gluconeogenesis → Glc-6-P → glucose
The liver rebuilds glucose, using 6 ATP-equivalents for every 2 ATP the muscle gained.
Glucose (top arrow) → muscle
Sent back to fuel more work.
Acetyl-CoA → TCA cycle (both tissues)
With enough O₂, pyruvate is oxidised instead. The liver's TCA activity, fed by fatty acids, provides the energy for gluconeogenesis.
Clinical / real-world · lactic acidosis

In shock or sepsis, tissues are starved of oxygen, so lactate production rises, and a failing liver clears less. Blood lactate is therefore a key bedside marker of tissue hypoperfusion. Metformin (which blocks hepatic gluconeogenesis, §6.2) can, rarely, cause lactic acidosis when kidney failure lets it accumulate, because the liver's Cori-cycle clearance of lactate is the very pathway it suppresses.

R Recall — anaerobic metabolism
  • Without O₂, pyruvate is converted to — lactate
  • Enzyme — lactate dehydrogenase
  • Purpose of making lactate — regenerate NAD⁺ so glycolysis continues
  • Lactate is recycled to glucose in the — liver by gluconeogenesis
  • Muscle–liver lactate/glucose loop — the Cori cycle

R Recall — the module's take-home points
  • Energy from carbohydrate oxidation is conserved as — high-energy bonds in ATP
  • Glucose breakdown begins with — anaerobic glycolysis → 2 pyruvate + 2 ATP + 2 NADH
  • With oxygen, pyruvate is — moved to the mitochondria and converted to acetyl-CoA
  • In the TCA, acetyl-CoA combines with — oxaloacetate to make citrate
  • ETC electron transfer to O₂ creates — a proton gradient that powers ATP synthase
  • Excess glucose is stored as — glycogen in liver and muscle (glycogenesis)

  • Gluconeogenesis makes glucose from — lactate, amino acids, glycerol once glycogen is exhausted
  • Cori cycle — when O₂ is limited, pyruvate → lactate to replenish NAD⁺; lactate feeds gluconeogenesis
